a001.heard: Every morning, a committee of egg farmers puts out one number. On twenty ninth October twenty twenty six, at Namakkal in Tamil Nadu, it was five rupees seventy paise for an egg.

a002.heard: Traders across India watch it. And yet Tamil Nadu is not even India's biggest egg state.

a003.heard: So how does one corner of the number two state end up setting the price? The answer starts with six hens that nobody wanted.

a006.heard: First, the place. Namakkal is a district in the middle of Tamil Nadu, just south of Salem. Until nineteen ninety seven it was part of Salem district.

a007.heard: India lays about one hundred and forty nine billion eggs a year, second only to China.

a008.heard: Andhra Pradesh lays the most, about eighteen in every hundred. Tamil Nadu is second, at about sixteen.

a009.heard: Inside Tamil Nadu, Namakkal is the giant. The state's own count gives it two of every three Tamil Nadu eggs. Even so, that is about one in ten of India's.

a010.heard: So it is not about volume alone. One egg in ten does not set the price for the other nine. The power of this place is something else. It is a price. And to see where that price came from, we go back to nineteen sixty nine.

a012.heard: In nineteen sixty nine, a village postmaster named V. Vellappan carried six red desi hens to the government veterinary hospital in Namakkal.

a013.heard: The vet, Doctor N. Nandagopal, looked at the six hens and suggested something else. Hybrid layers. More eggs. More manure for the fields. More income.

a014.heard: In nineteen seventy the vet drove Vellappan and three other farmers to a poultry firm in Coimbatore. They came back with four hundred chicks, at three or four rupees each.

a015.heard: Each farmer raised one hundred chicks in a small thatched shed. Every morning the vet came by to check them, free of cost.

a016.heard: The hens grew, and began to lay. And then the real problem? Nobody wanted their eggs.

a017.heard: The study says consumers and restaurant owners wanted only desi eggs.

a018.heard: Four farmers, each alone, with eggs nobody wanted. The vet's answer was simple. Form a club. Collect everyone's eggs. Sell them together.

a019.heard: The club sent eggs to Chennai by train and sold them for twenty two paise each.

a020.heard: Neighbours came to look, and sheds went up across the villages. By nineteen eighty two the area had about thirty lakh birds. By nineteen eighty five, seventy five lakh, and a veterinary college of its own.

a022.heard: But a farm full of hens has one weakness. Eggs do not wait. When too many arrive at once, the price falls, and every farmer stands alone against the buyer.

a023.heard: Around 1981, the committee's own history says, feed had become 250% dearer in five years, while an egg still sold for about 35 paise. More than 40% of poultry farmers had stopped.

a024.heard: A group of farmers, led by the breeder Doctor B. V. Rao, travelled the country and held more than three hundred meetings.

a025.heard: Their slogan, my egg, my price, my life.

a026.heard: On the fourteenth of May nineteen eighty two, the National Egg Coordination Committee began declaring egg prices. It is an association of poultry farmers, not a government body.

a027.heard: In Namakkal, farmers remember it more simply. P. K. Venkatachalam, one of the first, recalled taking a van of eggs to Chennai at an agreed nineteen paise. The trader offered fifteen. They settled at seventeen.

a028.heard: That is the click. Namakkal did not win by laying the most eggs. It won by being the place where farmers first agreed to say a price out loud.

a030.heard: But is it fair for producers to fix a price together? In twenty seventeen, two complaints reached the Competition Commission of India, one from a Namakkal resident, one from an animal welfare trust.

a031.heard: In January twenty twenty two the Commission gave its order. It found that the committee's price is the de facto price in the market, because no other body in India declares the price of eggs.

a032.heard: Nobody wanted their eggs in nineteen seventy. Fifty years later, nobody else was declaring a price.

a033.heard: It held that the committee had broken the competition law by trying to enforce its prices, with penalties or the threat of them. It ordered an end to such threats, and told the committee to say prominently that its prices are only suggestive.

a034.heard: It imposed no fine. The animal welfare trust appealed, asking for penalties and for the committee to be dissolved. In September twenty twenty two the appeals tribunal dismissed that appeal. A further appeal is pending in the Supreme Court.

a036.heard: So what is a suggestion worth? In July twenty twenty six, Namakkal's rate reached six rupees eighty paise, the highest on NECC's daily sheets since twenty twenty two.

a037.heard: Five weeks later it was five rupees twenty. Down about a quarter.

a038.heard: The world is buying more of India's eggs too. In twenty twenty five, official trade data show the most egg exports on record, nearly eighteen crore eggs a month. Then a Gulf crisis hit shipping, and in March twenty twenty six exports fell by seven tenths.

a039.heard: And every year the same shape. The rate dips in March and April, and climbs in November and December. In thirteen of sixteen years, the lowest month was March or April.

a040.heard: The club's first eggs sold for twenty two paise. The committee's suggestion this week is five rupees seventy. Not adjusted for inflation, but the same egg.

a041.heard: So both are true. Tamil Nadu is the number two egg state. And Namakkal's number is the one the trade reads first, because the farmers who once had no price made one.

a042.heard: Tomorrow morning there will be a new number. Printed under it, in small type, merely suggestive.
